title: Dominant affine group homomorphisms with reduced target are faithfully flat
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. A commutative Hopf $k$-algebra here means a unital commutative $k$-algebra $A$ with $k$-algebra maps $\Delta_A:A\to A\otimes_k A$, $\epsilon_A:A\to k$, $S_A:A\to A$ such that $(\Delta_A\otimes1)\Delta_A=(1\otimes\Delta_A)\Delta_A$, $(\epsilon_A\otimes1)\Delta_A=(1\otimes\epsilon_A)\Delta_A=1_A$, and $\mu_A(S_A\otimes1)\Delta_A=\mu_A(1\otimes S_A)\Delta_A=\eta_A\epsilon_A$, under the usual tensor unit and associativity identifications; $\mu_A$ and $\eta_A$ are multiplication and unit. Tensor products are those of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. A Hopf homomorphism $u:P\to Q$ means a $k$-algebra homomorphism with $\Delta_Qu=(u\otimes u)\Delta_P$, $\epsilon_Qu=\epsilon_P$ and $S_Qu=uS_P$. Let $A,B$ be commutative Hopf $k$-algebras, both finitely generated as $k$-algebras [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], and let $i:A\to B$ be an injective Hopf homomorphism. Assume $A$ is reduced, meaning that $a^n=0$ for $n\geq1$ implies $a=0$. Then $i$ is faithfully flat [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map]. No reducedness of $B$, connectedness, smoothness, or characteristic hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Corollary 1.69 and Proposition 1.70, printed p.28, with Proposition 1.65(a), pp.26--27, and the first paragraph of Theorem 3.31, p.73; their affine coordinate-algebra formulation.

proof.text: Put $G=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $H=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and $f=\operatorname{Spec}i$. By [lem-sfb-hopf-spectrum-functor], these are affine group schemes and $f$ is a homomorphism. The counits give $k$-points, so both schemes are nonempty. The finite algebra generators give finite-type structure maps and also make $B$ a finite-type $A$-algebra: the same generators work, since the image of $k$ lies in $i(A)$. Thus $f$ is finite type, using [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] and the quasi-compactness of affine schemes [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs]. The scheme $H$ is reduced by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-reduced-iff].

source.place: Corollary 1.69 and Proposition 1.70, p.28; Proposition 3.6, pp.66--67, coordinate interpretation.

proof.text: The morphism $f$ has dense image. Indeed its kernel sheaf on a principal open $D(a)\subset H$ is the kernel of $A_a\to B_{i(a)}$. If $r/a^n$ maps to zero, some $i(a)^m i(r)$ is zero; injectivity of $i$ gives $a^m r=0$, hence $r/a^n=0$. Principal opens form the defining affine basis, so the sheaf kernel is zero. As $f$ is quasi-compact, [lemma-nagata-scheme-image-ideal-qc] identifies the closure of its image with the vanishing locus of its kernel ideal, which is therefore all of $H$. This argument does not require $B$ reduced.

source.place: Corollary 1.69, p.28: dominance hypothesis, checked on coordinate rings; scheme-theoretic image formulation.

proof.text: By [lem-wf-affine-constructible-open], $f(G)$ is constructible and its density supplies a nonempty open $U\subset H$ contained in $f(G)$. We use [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space] to detect nonempty locally closed subsets of $G,H$ by closed points: write one as $Z\cap O$ with $Z$ closed and $O$ open; density of closed points in $Z$ gives a closed point in $Z\cap O$. By [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing](1), these closed points are $k$-points. Moreover every $k$-point $u\in f(G)$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=\ker(u:A\to k)$, lifts to $G(k)$: choose a prime $\mathfrak q\subset B$ with $i^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak m$ and a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n\supseteq\mathfrak q$ of $B$; then $i^{-1}(\mathfrak n)$ is a prime ideal containing the maximal $\mathfrak m$, so equals it. By the same assertion (1) for $B$, $\mathfrak n$ is the kernel of a $k$-algebra map $g:B\to k$, and $g\circ i:A\to k$ is a $k$-algebra map with kernel $\mathfrak m$, hence equals $u$ since $A/\mathfrak m=k$ as $k$-algebras. Thus $f(g)=u$; in particular $U(k)$ lifts. Put $S=f(G(k))\subset H(k)$. Thus $U(k)\subset S$. The subgroup property of $S$ follows from the homomorphism in step 1.

source.place: Proposition 1.68, p.28, and Proposition 1.65(b), p.27; explicit closed-point and fibre checks.

proof.text: For $s\in S$, left translation $L_s$ on $H$ is an isomorphism with inverse $L_{s^{-1}}$, by the group laws [def-sc-group-scheme]. Set $V=\bigcup_{s\in S}L_s(U)$. This is nonempty open. Choose $u_0\in U(k)$ by step 3. Its $k$-points are exactly $S$: containment in $S$ follows from $U(k)\subset S$, and $s=(s u_0^{-1})u_0$ proves the reverse. Hence $V$ contains all $k$-points of $U$ and all $S$. In fact $V$ contains $f(G)$: otherwise the constructible subset $f(G)\setminus V$ would contain a closed $k$-point by step 3, which lifts to $G(k)$ by the lifting argument of step 3 and so belongs to $S\subset V$, a contradiction. Density of $f(G)$ makes $V$ dense. If $y\in H(k)\setminus S$, then $V\cap L_y(V)$ is nonempty open because $V$ is dense. It has a $k$-point by step 3. Such a point lies both in $S=V(k)$ and in $yS=L_y(V)(k)$, contradicting disjointness of distinct cosets. Therefore $S=H(k)$.

source.place: Proposition 1.68 and Corollary 1.69, p.28; the open-subgroup/coset argument written out.

proof.text: The complement $H\setminus f(G)$ is constructible, since $f(G)$ is constructible by step 3. If nonempty, a locally closed piece of this complement has a closed $k$-point by the closed-point test of step 3. This contradicts $f(G(k))=H(k)$ from step 4. Thus $f$ is surjective on all underlying points, including nonclosed ones.

source.place: Corollary 1.69, p.28; passage from closed points to all points expanded.

proof.text: There is a nonempty open $U_0\subset H$ over which $f$ is flat. To see this without assuming $H$ irreducible, [lem-wf-affine-noetherian-components] gives finitely many irreducible components $C_1,\ldots,C_r$. Choose $C_1$ and let $W=H\setminus\bigcup_{j>1}C_j$. It is a nonempty open contained in $C_1$, hence irreducible: maximality of components prevents $C_1$ being covered by the other finitely many components. It is reduced since its local rings are those of the reduced $H$ [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Thus $W$ is integral by [def-pc-integral-scheme]. By [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change](2), $f^{-1}W\to W$ is finite type. Apply [lem-sbc-generic-flatness] to obtain a nonempty open $U_0\subset W$ with $f^{-1}U_0\to U_0$ flat. This is also an open of $H$.

source.place: Proposition 1.65(a), p.27, generic-flatness paragraph; component reduction makes the integral-base hypothesis explicit.

proof.text: Choose $u\in U_0(k)$ by step 3. For every $h\in H(k)$, step 4 gives $g\in G(k)$ with $f(g)=hu^{-1}$. The group laws give $f L_g=L_{f(g)}f$, and both translations are isomorphisms with inverses given by inverse elements [def-sc-group-scheme]. Hence the restriction over $L_{f(g)}U_0$ is isomorphic to the flat restriction over $U_0$. Explicitly, translation carries each local ring map to the same map conjugated by the induced local-ring isomorphisms; tensoring a module sequence after such ring isomorphisms has the same exactness, so flatness is preserved. By [def-weil-flat-morphism] it is flat at every point above this translated open. These opens contain every $h\in H(k)$, because $h=f(g)u$. Their union is all of $H$: its closed complement, if nonempty, has a closed $k$-point by step 3. Therefore $f$ is flat at every source point, hence flat. This uses no reducedness of $G$.

source.place: Proposition 1.65(a), p.27, translated-open cover; Proposition 1.70, p.28.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-affine-criterion] to the whole affine schemes $G,H$: the map on their coordinate rings is $i$, so $i$ is flat. Its prime-spectrum map is the surjective $f$ of step 5. Now [lem-weil-pbc-flat-surjective-spectrum-faithfully-flat] proves that $i$ is faithfully flat, exactly in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map]. All uses of reducedness were on $A$ or $H$, and the argument did not assume connectedness, smoothness or any characteristic restriction.

source.place: Proposition 1.70, p.28, concluding faithful flatness; affine criterion and algebraic faithful-flatness criterion.

proof_origin.place: Propositions 1.65(a), 1.68, Corollary 1.69 and Proposition 1.70, pp.26--28; coordinate-ring and closed-point details expanded.

Step 3 uses Chevalley (1)/(2), the Jacobson closed-point test and Nullstellensatz (1). Step 6 isolates an integral open component W, so the integral-base hypothesis of generic flatness holds; this is the only use of A reduced. Step 7 translates flatness using f L_g = L_{f(g)} f. Step 8 applies the affine flatness criterion and flat + Spec-surjective => faithfully flat. Edge cases checked: A=k, disconnected H, Frobenius k[t^p] in k[t], nonreduced B. The 3 recorded generic tool_uses (Chevalley, Nullstellensatz, generic flatness) are accepted.
